findings.title: Hardcoded API Key in Configuration
findings.impact: Credential exposure allowing unauthorized access to billing service; potential financial fraud and account compromise
findings.evidence: BILLING_API_KEY hardcoded as 'sk-acme-1f4d8e2b9c7a6d5e4f3b2a1c0d9e8f7a' in plaintext; compared to DOCS_TOKEN using environment variables, indicating inconsistent security practice
findings.recommendation: Move all API keys to environment variables via process.env or .env file; never commit credentials to version control; rotate exposed key immediately; implement secret scanning in CI/CD

findings.title: Shell Command Injection via Model Output
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution: attacker can manipulate model to generate malicious shell commands (RCE, data exfiltration, system compromise)
findings.evidence: Function summarize_and_run() executes model_output directly via subprocess.run(model_output, shell=True); shell=True enables shell metacharacter interpretation; no validation or sanitization of model output
findings.recommendation: Never execute user-controlled or model-generated input via shell=True; use subprocess.run([args], shell=False) with argument list instead; if shell features needed, parse and validate output before execution

findings.title: Unrestricted Tool Execution Without Permission Control
findings.impact: Horizontal privilege escalation: model can request refunds/lookups on arbitrary accounts without authorization
findings.evidence: run_tool() directly executes decision['tool'] and decision['account_id'] without checking session authentication; issue_refund() has no permission validation; vulnerable function is exposed despite safer run_tool_scoped() alternative existing in codebase
findings.recommendation: Use run_tool_scoped() instead of run_tool(); enforce account_id == session['authenticated_account_id'] for all operations; implement role-based access control (RBAC) for financial operations

findings.title: Prompt Injection via Unescaped User Input
findings.impact: Model instruction hijacking: attacker can inject override directives to bypass security constraints and manipulate model behavior
findings.evidence: build_prompt() concatenates docs and question directly without escaping; retrieved documents from ingest_ticket() are user-controlled; attacker can submit malicious ticket content or craft injection payload in question parameter
findings.recommendation: Use XML tagging (build_prompt_marked) or block-level content isolation; trust levels should filter untrusted content; implement prompt sandboxing to prevent instruction override; add model-level safeguards for injection detection

findings.title: Unsafe Dependency Execution via NPX
findings.impact: Supply chain attack: malicious package can be injected via npm registry compromise, typosquatting, or version compromise (RCE, backdoor, data theft)
findings.evidence: billing MCP uses 'npx -y @acme/billing-mcp@latest'; -y flag auto-executes without confirmation; @latest allows version drift; no integrity verification (SRI/hash); package executed with full application process privileges
findings.recommendation: Pin exact version (not @latest); use npm ci instead of npm install for reproducible builds; implement package.json lock files; verify package integrity with npm audit; consider package signing and allowlisting trusted publishers

findings.title: Unvalidated Model Output Stored Persistently
findings.impact: Denial of Service and data pollution: model output can fill storage, pollute persistence layer, or grow unbounded
findings.evidence: remember_from_reply() appends model reply to notes[] with no validation, size limits, or content checks; attacker can induce model to generate multi-GB responses causing disk exhaustion
findings.recommendation: Implement output size limits (e.g., max 10KB per reply); validate content before storage; implement quota management; add rate limiting for storage operations; monitor file size growth

findings.title: Missing File Permission Controls on Sensitive Data
findings.impact: Local information disclosure: JSON file permissions default to umask, allowing other users/processes to read customer data, preferences, and ticket contents
findings.evidence: STORE = Path('/var/lib/acme/agent-memory.json'); write_text() uses default permissions (typically 0o644); no explicit chmod() call; file contains customer tickets, preferences, and persistent notes
findings.recommendation: Explicitly set file permissions to 0o600 after writes: STORE.chmod(0o600); use os.open() with mode parameter; implement file locking for concurrent access safety; verify permissions in tests
